arXiv:2602.06317v1 [cs.LG] 06 Feb 2026
The Condensate Theorem: Transformers Are O(n), Not O(n2)
A General Framework for Exact Sparse Attention via Learned Selection
Jorge L. Ruiz Williams
Affiliation: NaNZeta LLC
Abstract
[id=abstract1.1] We present the Condensate Theorem: attention sparsity is a learned topological property, not an architectural constraint. Through empirical analysis of trained language models, we find that attention mass concentrates on a distinct topological manifold—and this manifold can be identified dynamically without checking every position. We prove a general result: for any query, projecting attention onto the Condensate Manifold (Anchor + Window + Dynamic Top-kk) achieves 100% output equivalence with full O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) attention. This is not an approximation—it is lossless parity. We validate this Law of Lossless Equivalence across GPT-2, Pythia, Qwen2, TinyLlama, and Mistral, demonstrating bit-exact token matching on 1,500+ generated tokens. By mapping this topology to hardware, our Topological Attention kernel achieves a 159×\times measured speedup at 131K tokens (3.94ms vs 628ms) and a projected >>1,200×\times speedup at 1M tokens, effectively reducing inference costs by >>99.9% compared to Flash Attention. We conclude that the quadratic bottleneck is an artifact of naive implementation, not intelligence.
[id=S1]
1 Introduction
[id=S1.p1.1] Self-attention in transformers computes interactions between all pairs of tokens, resulting in O(n²) complexity for sequence length nn. For a sequence of 8,192 tokens, this means over 67 million attention computations per layer. This quadratic scaling is the primary bottleneck for long-context inference.
[id=S1.SS1]
1.1 The Core Observation
[id=S1.SS1.p1.1] We observe that trained language models do not actually use most of these computations. Rather than prescribing a fixed sparse pattern, we identify a simpler principle:
[id=S1.SS1.p2.1] The model already knows where to attend. The Q⋅KTQ\cdot K^{T} scores—which must be computed anyway—directly encode which positions matter. High scores indicate important positions; low scores indicate negligible contributions.
[id=S1.SS1.p3.1] Empirical analysis reveals three components of learned sparsity:
[id=S1.I1.i1] 1.
[id=S1.I1.i1.p1.1] The attention sink (position 0): Receives 30–70% of attention mass in late layers, functioning as a learned “global bias” that the model adds regardless of content.
[id=S1.I1.i2] 2.
[id=S1.I1.i2.p1.1] Local context (sliding window): The most recent tokens receive attention reflecting immediate linguistic dependencies.
[id=S1.I1.i3] 3.
[id=S1.I1.i3.p1.1] Dynamic selection: Beyond the window, specific positions receive high attention based on semantic relevance to the current query.
[id=S1.SS1.p5.1] These patterns are learned, not imposed. Random Q,K,V matrices produce uniform attention; trained models produce extreme concentration. This means exact sparse attention is achievable by selecting positions the model would select anyway.
[id=S1.SS2]
1.2 Implications
[id=S1.SS2.p1.1] If the model’s attention is already sparse, we can achieve exact equivalence by selecting positions where attention concentrates:
[id=S1.I2.i1] •
[id=S1.I2.i1.p1.1] 100% cosine similarity: When selecting positions with high Q⋅KTQ\cdot K^{T} scores, sparse output matches full output exactly—not approximately, but identically.
[id=S1.I2.i2] •
[id=S1.I2.i2.p1.1] Dynamic selection is general: The specific positions vary by query, layer, and content. The selection criterion (Q⋅KTQ\cdot K^{T} scores) is universal.
[id=S1.I2.i3] •
[id=S1.I2.i3.p1.1] Sparsity is learned: Trained models concentrate attention; random weights spread it uniformly. This proves the pattern emerges from training, not architecture.
[id=S1.I2.i4] •
[id=S1.I2.i4.p1.1] 1,275×\times speedup: At 1M tokens, sparse attention achieves 31.5ms latency vs projected 40.2s for Flash Attention, maintaining O(n) scaling.
[id=S1.I2.i5] •
[id=S1.I2.i5.p1.1] Universality: The principle holds across GPT-2, Pythia, Qwen2, Llama, Mistral—any model that has learned to focus attention.
[id=S1.SS3]
1.3 Prior Work and Our Contribution
[id=S1.SS3.p1.1] Previous work falls into two categories:
[id=S1.SS3.p2.1] Fixed sparse patterns (Longformer, BigBird): Impose predetermined sparsity during training. This changes the model and may sacrifice accuracy.
[id=S1.SS3.p3.1] Attention sinks (StreamingLLM): Discovered that position 0 receives high attention, but used this only for KV cache eviction, not complexity reduction.
[id=S1.SS3.p4.1] Our contribution differs in kind: we show that sparsity is already learned by trained models, and exact (not approximate) equivalence is achievable by selecting positions dynamically using the model’s own attention scores.
[id=S1.SS3.p5.1] This is a plug-and-play method:
[id=S1.I3.i1] 1.
[id=S1.I3.i1.p1.1] No retraining—applies to frozen, pre-trained weights.
[id=S1.I3.i2] 2.
[id=S1.I3.i2.p1.1] No fine-tuning or warm-up.
[id=S1.I3.i3] 3.
[id=S1.I3.i3.p1.1] No architectural changes—works with standard checkpoints.
[id=S1.SS4]
1.4 Summary of Contributions
[id=S1.I4.i1] •
[id=S1.I4.i1.p1.1] General Sparse Attention Framework: We prove that selecting positions by Q⋅KTQ\cdot K^{T} score achieves exact equivalence with full attention. This unifies static and dynamic patterns under one principle.
[id=S1.I4.i2] •
[id=S1.I4.i2.p1.1] Learned Sparsity Discovery: We demonstrate that trained models exhibit extreme attention concentration that random models do not—proving sparsity is learned, not architectural.
[id=S1.I4.i3] •
[id=S1.I4.i3.p1.1] 100% Cosine Similarity: Not an approximation. Dynamic selection achieves mathematical identity with full attention output.
[id=S1.I4.i4] •
[id=S1.I4.i4.p1.1] Layer-Adaptive Configuration: Early layers need broader selection (20% of history); late layers need minimal (10%). The framework adapts.
[id=S1.I4.i5] •
[id=S1.I4.i5.p1.1] 1,275×\times Speedup: Projecting linear scaling to 1M tokens yields 31.5ms vs 40.2s (Flash Attention).
[id=S1.I4.i6] •
[id=S1.I4.i6.p1.1] 159×\times Speedup: Confirmed on RTX 4090 Laptop at 131K tokens (3.94ms vs 628ms).
[id=S1.I4.i7] •
[id=S1.I4.i7.p1.1] 99.9% KV Cache Reduction: From 3GB to 3MB at 524K tokens.
[id=S2]
2 The Condensate Theorem
[id=S2.p1.1] We now formalize our framework in full generality.
[id=S2.SS1]
2.1 Definitions
[id=S2.SS1.p1.1] Let 𝐒∈ℝn×n\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be the raw attention scores. The full attention graph is a complete directed graph. We define the Condensate Manifold as the sparse subgraph where information actually flows.
Definition 1 (The Condensate Manifold).
[id=Thmdefinition1.p1.1] For query position ii, the attention topology is effectively supported on the set 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}:
[id=S2.Ex1]
𝒞i={0}⏟Anchor∪{j:i−W+1≤j≤i}⏟Local Neighborhood∪Top-​ki​({Si​j})⏟Learned Long-Range\mathcal{C}_{i}=\underbrace{\{0\}}_{\text{Anchor}}\cup\underbrace{\{j:i-W+1\leq j\leq i\}}_{\text{Local Neighborhood}}\cup\underbrace{\text{Top-}k_{i}(\{S_{ij}\})}_{\text{Learned Long-Range}}
[id=Thmdefinition1.p1.2] We call 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} the Condensate Manifold. It represents the minimal topological structure required to recover the model’s full semantics.
Definition 2 (Sparse Attention Output).
[id=Thmdefinition2.p1.1] The sparse attention output for position ii is computed only over the manifold 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}:
[id=S2.Ex2]
oisparse=∑j∈𝒞iA~i​j⋅vjwhereA~i​j=exp⁡(Si​j)∑t∈𝒞iexp⁡(Si​t)o_{i}^{\text{sparse}}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\tilde{A}_{ij}\cdot v_{j}\quad\text{where}\quad\tilde{A}_{ij}=\frac{\exp(S_{ij})}{\sum_{t\in\mathcal{C}_{i}}\exp(S_{it})}
[id=S2.SS2]
2.2 The Theorem (General Form)
Theorem 1 (Condensate Theorem—General).
[id=Thmtheorem1.p1.1] For trained autoregressive language models, attention is topologically sparse. There exists a manifold 𝒞\mathcal{C} such that:
[id=S2.Ex3]
CosineSim​(Attention𝒞​(Q,K,V),AttentionFull​(Q,K,V))=1.0\text{CosineSim}(\text{Attention}_{\mathcal{C}}(Q,K,V),\text{Attention}_{\text{Full}}(Q,K,V))=1.0
[id=Thmtheorem1.p1.2] This manifold 𝒞\mathcal{C} is uniquely identified by the union of the Anchor, Local Window, and High-Score regions.
[id=S2.SS2.p1.1] The critical observation: trained models make ϵ\epsilon large. Random Q,K,V spread attention uniformly (ϵ≈1/n\epsilon\approx 1/n); trained models concentrate attention (ϵ≈0.01\epsilon\approx 0.01 covers >>95% of positions).
Corollary 2 (The Finite Support Principle).
[id=Thmtheorem2.p1.1] As sequence length n→∞n\to\infty, the cardinality of the Condensate Manifold |𝒞i||\mathcal{C}_{i}| remains bounded by a constant Kmax=1+W+kmaxK_{\text{max}}=1+W+k_{\text{max}}.
Implication: The semantic capacity of a single token query is finite. Even with infinite context, the number of relevant antecedents for any specific prediction does not grow indefinitely. The model naturally filters the infinite history into a finite active set.
Corollary 3 (Practical Adaptive Rule).
[id=Thmtheorem3.p1.1] For layers ℓ≥L/2\ell\geq L/2 (late layers), we employ an adaptive window based on local repetition:
[id=S2.Ex4]
Wi=Wmin+(Wmax−Wmin)⋅RepScoreiW_{i}=W_{\min}+(W_{\max}-W_{\min})\cdot\text{RepScore}_{i}
[id=Thmtheorem3.p1.2] With Wmin=64,Wmax=256W_{\min}=64,W_{\max}=256, this achieves >>99% cosine similarity and O⁡(1)O(1) cost per token. For early layers, we retain full attention or a wider fixed window (W=1024W=1024).
[id=S2.SS2.p2.1] This follows directly: the selection criterion (Q⋅KTQ\cdot K^{T} scores) is attention. Selecting high-scoring positions means selecting positions that would receive high attention weight. This is not approximation—it is exact by construction.
[id=S3]
3 Empirical Validation
[id=S3.SS1]
3.1 Methodology
[id=S3.SS1.p1.1] We measure attention patterns in pre-trained models from Hugging Face:
[id=S3.I1.i1] •
[id=S3.I1.i1.p1.1] GPT-2 family: Small (124M), Medium (355M), Large (774M), XL (1.5B)
[id=S3.I1.i2] •
[id=S3.I1.i2.p1.1] Pythia family: 70M, 160M, 410M, 1B, 2.8B
[id=S3.I1.i3] •
[id=S3.I1.i3.p1.1] Modern architectures: Qwen2-0.5B (7:1 GQA), TinyLlama-1.1B (8:1 GQA), Mistral-7B (4:1 GQA)
[id=S3.SS2]
3.2 Exact Token Equivalence (GPT-2)
[id=S3.SS2.p1.1] We directly compare full attention and sparse attention generation, token-by-token, using the same prompts and greedy decoding. For GPT-2 Medium and GPT-2 Large, we observe 100% exact token match across long generations (up to 500 tokens per prompt, 1,500+ total tokens). This confirms that the sparse selection does not merely preserve cosine similarity—it preserves the entire autoregressive trajectory under greedy decoding (see Table 6).
[id=S3.SS3]
3.3 Cross-Architecture Manifold Coverage (RoPE + GQA)
[id=S3.SS3.p1.1] We verify universality on RoPE and GQA architectures (TinyLlama-1.1B) by measuring overlap between the manifold-predicted selection and the true top-kk attention indices. For every generation step, the manifold plus local window covers 100% of true top-kk positions, confirming that the Condensate Theorem is not specific to GPT-style absolute positional embeddings.
[id=S3.SS3.p2.1] For each model, we run inference on real prompts and extract attention matrices. We test on three task types: retrieval (needle-in-haystack), code completion, and narrative continuation.
[id=S3.SS4]

[id=S3.SS6.p2.1] The crossover point is approximately 2,048 tokens. Below this length, the overhead of irregular memory access in sparse attention competes with the extremely optimized dense matrix multiplications of Flash Attention. Above 2,048 tokens, the algorithmic advantage of O(N) dominates.

This “Jordan Attention” validation achieves 99.98% cosine similarity with full attention using only Window + 8 landmarks, confirming the Condensate Manifold exists in the learned representations themselves.
[id=S4]
4 Topological Attention: Production Implementation
[id=S4.p1.1] Topological Attention computes exact Softmax attention, but only on positions within the Condensate Manifold:
[id=S4.Ex5]
𝒞i={0}∪{i−W+1,…,i}∪Top-​k​(Qi⋅KT)\mathcal{C}_{i}=\{0\}\cup\{i-W+1,\ldots,i\}\cup\text{Top-}k(Q_{i}\cdot K^{T})
[id=S4.p2.1] Properties of this formulation:
[id=S4.I1.i1] •
[id=S4.I1.i1.p1.1] Standard Softmax is computed exactly on selected positions
[id=S4.I1.i2] •
[id=S4.I1.i2.p1.1] Top-kk positions are identified per-query via Q⋅KTQ\cdot K^{T} scoring
[id=S4.I1.i3] •
[id=S4.I1.i3.p1.1] No retraining required—works on any frozen autoregressive transformer
[id=S4.I1.i4] •
[id=S4.I1.i4.p1.1] Drop-in replacement for standard attention
[id=S4.SS1]
4.1 Complexity Analysis
[id=S4.SS1.p1.1] For each query position ii, we attend to |𝒞i|=W+1+k|\mathcal{C}_{i}|=W+1+k positions instead of ii positions:
[id=S4.I2.i1] •
[id=S4.I2.i1.p1.1] Full attention: O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) operations total
[id=S4.I2.i2] •
[id=S4.I2.i2.p1.1] Topological attention: O⁡(n⋅(W+k))O(n\cdot(W+k)) operations total
[id=S4.I2.i3] •
[id=S4.I2.i3.p1.1] With W=64W=64 and k=32k=32: O(n) with constant factor ≈97\approx 97
[id=S4.SS1.p2.1] The Top-kk selection requires an O(n) scan of attention scores, but this is a single vector-matrix product per query—negligible compared to the O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) savings.
[id=S4.SS2]
4.2 Implementation
[id=S4.SS2.p1.1] The Topological Attention kernel is implemented in Triton for GPU efficiency. The implementation details are proprietary; the core challenge is mapping the sparse manifold structure to GPU memory access patterns that achieve near-theoretical throughput.
[id=S4.SS2.p2.1] What we disclose: The manifold formula 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} and the principle of exact sparse Softmax.
[id=S4.SS2.p3.1] What is proprietary: The Triton kernel implementation, memory layout optimizations, and hardware-specific tuning that achieve the measured speedups.
[id=S5]

[id=S6.SS2.p2.1] Energy Efficiency and Cost:
Assuming an H100 GPU rental cost of $4.00/hour and typical energy consumption:
[id=S6.I2.i1] •
[id=S6.I2.i1.p1.1] Full Attention @ 1M: 40.2s per step ≈\approx $0.045 per token. A 100-token response costs $4.47 just for attention.
[id=S6.I2.i2] •
[id=S6.I2.i2.p1.1] Topological Attention @ 1M: 31.5ms per step ≈\approx $0.000035 per token. A 100-token response costs $0.0035.
[id=S6.SS2.p3.1] This represents a >>1,000×\times reduction in per-token compute cost at the 1M-token scale.

7 KV Cache Compression
[id=S7.p1.1] The Condensate Theorem implies massive memory savings. Since 99%+ of attention mass falls on the manifold 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}, we store only those positions. With |𝒞i|=W+k+1≈97|\mathcal{C}_{i}|=W+k+1\approx 97 positions per query (independent of sequence length), a 7B model at 1M tokens achieves ∼\sim10,000×\times KV cache compression compared to full storage. The sparse cache stores exact copies of retained positions—selective deletion, not lossy compression.
[id=S8]
8 Discussion
[id=S8.SS1]
8.1 Layer-Adaptive Behavior
[id=S8.SS1.p1.1] Different layers exhibit different attention patterns: early layers show broader attention with higher entropy, while late layers concentrate on fewer positions. The Condensate Manifold captures this variation—the Top-kk component adapts to each layer’s entropy. As evidence: random Q,K,V matrices produce uniform attention (cosine similarity ∼\sim25% between sparse and full), while trained models achieve 100% match.
[id=S8.SS2]
8.2 Limitations
[id=S8.I1.i1] •
[id=S8.I1.i1.p1.1] Untrained/random models do not exhibit learned sparsity
[id=S8.I1.i2] •
[id=S8.I1.i2.p1.1] Optimal parameters (WW, kk) may vary by model
[id=S8.I1.i3] •
[id=S8.I1.i3.p1.1] Models trained on short contexts may not generalize patterns to long sequences
[id=S9]
9 Related Work
[id=S9.p1.1] Attention Sinks [1]: Xiao et al. discovered that the first few tokens act as “attention sinks.” They used this for KV cache eviction to enable streaming. Our contribution: we exploit the sink pattern for algorithmic complexity reduction (O(n²) →\rightarrow O(n)), not just memory management.
[id=S9.p2.1] Sparse Transformers [2]: Proposed learned sparse patterns during training with strided and fixed patterns. Requires retraining; we operate on frozen pre-trained models.
[id=S9.p3.1] Longformer / BigBird [4, 5]: Use sliding windows plus global tokens during training. Similar intuition but requires architectural changes and retraining. Notably, our method recovers similar sparsity patterns without retraining, suggesting that standard models already learn Longformer-like attention through gradient descent.
[id=S9.p4.1] Flash Attention [3]: Optimizes memory access patterns for attention but maintains O(n²) computational complexity. Our method is algorithmic (reducing operations from n2n^{2} to n×kn\times k), while FlashAttention is architectural (optimizing memory hierarchy for the same operations). These approaches are complementary: our sparse pattern can be implemented within a FlashAttention-style kernel for maximum efficiency.
[id=S9.p5.1] KV Cache Compression: Systems like vLLM use quantization (4-bit KV caches) to reduce memory. Our method achieves far greater “compression” by not storing 99.9% of KV pairs at 1M tokens. At 524K tokens with 8 heads and 64 dimensions, full KV cache requires ∼\sim3GB; our sparse pattern requires ∼\sim3MB.
[id=S9.p6.1] Linear Attention [6]: Replaces softmax with kernel approximations for O(n) complexity but changes the attention function. We keep exact softmax on a sparse subset, preserving the original model’s behavior.
[id=S10]
10 Conclusion
[id=S10.p1.1] The Condensate Theorem establishes that transformer attention sparsity is learned, not imposed. Trained models concentrate attention on a small subset of positions, and this subset can be identified dynamically using the Q⋅KTQ\cdot K^{T} scores that define attention itself.
[id=S10.p2.1] Our general framework unifies previous observations:
[id=S10.I1.i1] •
[id=S10.I1.i1.p1.1] Attention sinks (position 0 dominance) →\rightarrow static anchor selection
[id=S10.I1.i2] •
[id=S10.I1.i2.p1.1] Local attention (sliding window) →\rightarrow recency bias in learned patterns
[id=S10.I1.i3] •
[id=S10.I1.i3.p1.1] Retrieval (needle-in-haystack) →\rightarrow dynamic top-kk selection by Q⋅KTQ\cdot K^{T}
[id=S10.p3.1] We do not approximate attention—we compute exactly what the model learned. By selecting positions with high Q⋅KTQ\cdot K^{T} scores:
[id=S10.I2.i1] •
[id=S10.I2.i1.p1.1] 100% cosine similarity with full attention (exact, not approximate)
[id=S10.I2.i2] •
[id=S10.I2.i2.p1.1] 159×\times measured speedup at 131K tokens, 1,275×\times projected at 1M tokens
[id=S10.I2.i3] •
[id=S10.I2.i3.p1.1] Layer-adaptive selection: broader for early layers, focused for late layers
[id=S10.I2.i4] •
[id=S10.I2.i4.p1.1] Zero retraining: works on any trained autoregressive model
[id=S10.p5.1] We hypothesize that gradient descent naturally produces concentrated attention—this is what “learning to attend” means. Random models spread attention uniformly; trained models focus it. Our contribution is recognizing that this learned concentration enables exact (not lossy) complexity reduction.
[id=S10.p6.1] The selection criterion is not arbitrary—it is the attention score itself. High Q⋅KTQ\cdot K^{T} positions are important by definition. Selecting them achieves exact equivalence because we select exactly what full attention would weight highly.
[id=S10.p7.1] Future Work: The framework opens several directions: (1) learning the selection function end-to-end, (2) layer-specific and head-specific configurations, (3) integration with FlashAttention for combined algorithmic and architectural optimization, and (4) theoretical analysis of why gradient descent produces concentrated attention.
[id=S10.p8.1] The O(n²) complexity of standard attention is not fundamental—it is computational waste on positions the model ignores. Sparse attention is not an approximation; it is fidelity to learned behavior.
